content.value: Linux is an open-source operating system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991. Unlike Windows or macOS, Linux is free, highly customizable, and powers the vast majority of the world's servers, cloud infrastructure, and DevOps tooling.

When people say "Linux", they usually mean a **Linux distribution** (distro) — a complete OS built on the Linux kernel. Popular distros include Ubuntu, CentOS, Alpine, and Debian. In DevOps, you'll encounter Alpine (lightweight containers) and Ubuntu (general-purpose servers) most often.
Over 96% of the world's top 1 million servers run Linux. Every major cloud provider (AWS, GCP, Azure) defaults to Linux instances. Knowing Linux is non-negotiable for DevOps.

content.title: Linux Architecture
content.value:
Hardware → Kernel → System Libraries → Shell → Applications

The kernel manages hardware resources. The shell (bash/zsh) is your interface to interact with the kernel via commands.

quiz.question: What percentage of top servers run Linux?
quiz.explanation: Over 96% of the world's top 1 million servers run Linux, making it the dominant server operating system.

content.value: Linux organizes everything as files in a tree structure starting from the root directory `/`. Unlike Windows drive letters (C:, D:), Linux has a single unified tree.

content.title: Key Directories
content.value:
/          Root of the filesystem
/home      User home directories
/etc       Configuration files
/var       Variable data (logs, databases)
/tmp       Temporary files (cleared on reboot)
/usr       User programs and utilities
/bin       Essential command binaries
/opt       Optional/third-party software
You navigate using these essential commands:

content.title: Navigation Commands
content.value:
pwd                    # Print Working Directory — where am I?
ls                     # List files in current directory
ls -la                 # List ALL files (including hidden) with details
cd /home/student       # Change Directory to an absolute path
cd ..                  # Go up one level
cd ~                   # Go to your home directory
cd -                   # Go back to previous directory
Use Tab for auto-completion. Type 'cd /ho' then press Tab — it completes to 'cd /home/'. This saves massive time.

quiz.question: What does the command 'cd ..' do?
quiz.explanation: 'cd ..' moves you one level up in the directory tree. '..' always refers to the parent directory.

content.value: Creating, copying, moving, and deleting files are the bread and butter of Linux administration. Here are the core commands:

content.title: Creating Files and Directories
content.value:
touch file.txt              # Create an empty file
mkdir mydir                 # Create a directory
mkdir -p a/b/c              # Create nested directories in one shot
echo 'Hello' > file.txt     # Write text to a file (overwrites)
echo 'World' >> file.txt    # Append text to a file

content.title: Copying, Moving, and Deleting
content.value:
cp file.txt backup.txt      # Copy a file
cp -r dir1 dir2             # Copy a directory recursively
mv old.txt new.txt          # Rename a file
mv file.txt /tmp/           # Move a file to another location
rm file.txt                 # Delete a file
rm -r mydir                 # Delete a directory and its contents
rm -rf mydir                # Force delete without prompts

rm -rf is extremely dangerous — it deletes everything without asking. In interviews, always mention that you would use 'rm -i' (interactive) or double-check paths before running destructive commands. This shows production awareness.

content.title: Reading Files
content.value:
cat file.txt                # Print entire file content
head -n 5 file.txt          # Print first 5 lines
tail -n 5 file.txt          # Print last 5 lines
tail -f /var/log/syslog     # Follow a log file in real-time
less file.txt               # Paginated file viewer (q to quit)
wc -l file.txt              # Count lines in a file

quiz.question: What is the difference between '>' and '>>' in bash?
options: No difference, both write to files
'>' overwrites the file, '>>' appends to it
'>' appends to the file, '>>' overwrites it
'>' is for files, '>>' is for directories
quiz.explanation: '>' (redirect) overwrites the entire file with new content. '>>' (append) adds new content to the end of the file without removing existing content.

content.value: Linux uses a permission system to control who can read, write, or execute files. Every file has three permission groups: **owner** (u), **group** (g), and **others** (o).

content.title: Reading Permission Strings
content.value:
-rwxr-xr--  1  student  devops  4096  Jan 1 12:00  script.sh
 │││ ││││││
 │││ │││└┘└── Others: r-- (read only)
 │││ └┘└──── Group:  r-x (read + execute)
 └┘└────── Owner:  rwx (read + write + execute)
 └──────── File type: - (file) or d (directory)

content.title: Changing Permissions
content.value:
chmod +x script.sh          # Add execute permission for all
chmod 755 script.sh         # Owner: rwx, Group: r-x, Others: r-x
chmod 644 config.txt        # Owner: rw-, Group: r--, Others: r--
chown student:devops file   # Change owner and group
The numeric system: r=4, w=2, x=1. Add them up per group. So 755 means owner=7(rwx), group=5(r-x), others=5(r-x). This is asked in almost every DevOps interview.

quiz.question: What does chmod 644 mean?
options: Owner can read/write, group and others can read only
Owner can read/write/execute, others have no access
Only the owner can access the file
quiz.explanation: 644 = Owner: 6 (rw-), Group: 4 (r--), Others: 4 (r--). The owner can read and write, everyone else can only read.

content.value: Every running program in Linux is a **process** with a unique Process ID (PID). Understanding processes is essential for debugging servers, managing resources, and troubleshooting in production.

content.title: Viewing Processes
content.value:
ps aux                      # List all running processes
ps aux | grep nginx         # Find a specific process
top                         # Real-time process monitor
htop                        # Better interactive process monitor

content.title: Managing Processes
content.value:
kill 1234                   # Send SIGTERM to PID 1234 (graceful)
kill -9 1234                # Send SIGKILL (force kill — last resort)
killall nginx               # Kill all processes named 'nginx'
nohup ./server.sh &         # Run in background, survives logout
jobs                        # List background jobs
fg %1                       # Bring job 1 to foreground
Interview tip: Always explain that you'd try 'kill' (SIGTERM) before 'kill -9' (SIGKILL). SIGTERM lets the process clean up gracefully. SIGKILL is a last resort. This shows production maturity.

quiz.question: What is the difference between kill and kill -9?
options: kill sends SIGTERM (graceful), kill -9 sends SIGKILL (force)
kill works on files, kill -9 works on processes
quiz.explanation: 'kill' sends SIGTERM which asks the process to shut down gracefully (save state, close connections). 'kill -9' sends SIGKILL which immediately terminates the process with no cleanup.
